raw_response:
I’m going to keep most of my land in the usual pattern because that is what fits our place and our timing. On the better fields with easier irrigation, I’ll do wheat followed by summer maize. That system keeps cash coming in twice and spreads risk better than putting everything into one crop. I’ll leave part of the land in cotton because cotton still gives me another income channel, and on 225 mu I can manage a split system with machinery and hired help at the busy points. I have some schooling, so I do look at rates and costs more carefully than older farmers around me, but I still don’t gamble. If fertilizer and water are expensive, I would rather hold a solid yield than chase the very highest one.

For winter wheat, I’ll sow in early to mid October on about 150 mu. I want a uniform stand, so I’ll use a locally available improved variety and put most of the phosphorus down as base fertilizer, then split nitrogen between base and jointing. Wheat responds to water here, but pumping costs money, so I’ll plan three irrigations unless rainfall is unusually good. Once wheat is harvested in June, I’ll move fast into summer maize on the same 150 mu. The turnaround is tight, so I’ll use rotary tillage or direct seeding after wheat harvest depending on how quickly I can get the machine. For maize I’ll use hybrid seed, keep nitrogen moderate but not low, and usually irrigate once or twice depending on rain. Cotton will stay on 75 mu. It needs more management across the season, but on my farm size I can still handle it if I hire some labor during the picking period. I won’t overpush fertilizer on cotton because the return is less certain than wheat and maize, and too much vegetative growth is not what I want.
